about: The shipping library (PRD A4, 2026-11-10): published findings the lines across records (FR-T9.3) and the reading (FR-T9.9) may cite. Each entry gives the sentence the product may show, its citation, its address, the date it was opened and how it was read. Only entries with ships = true are ever used. No entry is added in the build.

entries.sentence: 834 people rated 129 reasons for listening to music. The reasons fell into three groups: mood and energy, self-awareness, and social connection. The first two were judged much more important than the third.
entries.citation: Schäfer, Sedlmeier, Städtler & Huron 2013, Frontiers in Psychology 4:511

entries.sentence: Among 80 people choosing the records they would keep, half of the choices had mattered most between the ages of 10 and 30, and the commonest reason was a memory of a person, a period or a place.
entries.citation: Loveday, Woy & Conway 2020, Quarterly Journal of Experimental Psychology 73(11)

entries.sentence: 470 adults aged 18 to 82 rated songs from across their lives. Music-related memories peaked for songs from around the age of 14, and young adults also rated music from their parents' teenage years highly.
entries.citation: Jakubowski, Eerola, Tillmann, Perrin & Heine 2020, Music & Science 3

entries.not_shipped_because: read only through a summary page; the paper itself could not be opened
entries.sentence: A study of adolescents found seven ways they use music to manage mood, among them mental work and solace.
374 people rated social reasons for turning to music, television and fiction. The reasons formed seven groups, among them company, understanding others and reminiscence.

In a survey of 772 people, the rewards of listening to sad music were imagination, emotion regulation, empathy and having no real-life implications. Nostalgia, more than sadness, was what sad music most often brought.
When people heard excerpts of popular songs from their past, about three in ten of the excerpts brought back a memory of their own life.

entries.not_shipped_because: taken from the old project's blueprint, not re-opened at its source
entries.sentence: People put in a bad mood chose energetic, joyful music for longer.
In an experiment, changing a piece's tempo changed how alert listeners felt and not their mood, and changing its mode, major or minor, changed their mood and not how alert they felt.
When repetition was added to unfamiliar music, listeners rated it more enjoyable, interesting and artistic.
entries.citation: Margulis 2013, Empirical Studies of the Arts 31(1), 45–57

entries.not_shipped_because: read only through the publisher's press release; the paper was not opened
entries.sentence: After the loss of a relationship, people preferred sad music more than after a loss of another kind.
entries.citation: Lee, Andrade & Palmer 2013, Journal of Consumer Research

entries.label: philosophy, from a secondary source
entries.sentence: A philosopher's account, not a study: for R. G. Collingwood, "To express is to become conscious of an emotion", and artists "speak to those who understand", expressing "emotions that are mutually held".
entries.citation: Kemp, "Collingwood's Aesthetics", Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, revised 2021-11-30 (on Collingwood's The Principles of Art, 1938)
